fanOut.question: What are the key architectural differences between monolithic and microservices application architectures, and under what circumstances is each typically preferred?
fanOut.findings: Monoliths package logic/data/UI into one deployed process; microservices decompose into independently owned, API/event-connected services. Tradeoffs: (1) deployment/ops - monolith is simpler to release as a unit but forces coordinated releases, microservices deploy independently but need distributed tracing/orchestration; (2) scaling - monolith scales as a whole (wasteful), microservices scale per-service but add network latency; (3) team autonomy - monolith needs shared codebase ownership, microservices let small teams own services end-to-end but require clear contracts. Rule of thumb: start monolithic for small teams/young projects/tight latency needs; adopt microservices once independent team scaling or deployment conflicts become the bottleneck and operational maturity exists. Modular monoliths are a middle ground worth evaluating first.

fanOut.question: What are the main security best practices for storing and handling user passwords in a web application (hashing algorithms, salting, and related guidance)?
fanOut.findings: Use memory-hard, adaptive hashing algorithms - Argon2 (OWASP-preferred), bcrypt, or scrypt - never fast general-purpose hashes like MD5/SHA-1, which are cryptographically broken and cheaply brute-forced. Every password needs a unique, random salt (16+ bytes) to defeat rainbow tables and ensure identical passwords hash differently per user; bcrypt/Argon2 handle this internally. Additional practices: an optional server-side pepper for defense-in-depth, rate limiting/account lockout to throttle brute-force attempts, and never logging plaintext passwords.
